entries.text:
To the Directorate of Estates,
New Delhi

7 December 2026

Subject: Representation regarding the occupancy of the allotted bungalow on Tughlak Road.

Sir,

I submit this representation in response to the query raised regarding my occupancy of the premises allotted to Shri G. Hegde, Joint Secretary. The purpose of this document is to clarify the facts of my presence and to account for the discrepancy in identity, which arises not from malice but from a clerical error of substitution that I am now compelled to rectify in the eyes of the administration.

I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, a philosopher. I do not claim to be Shri G. Hegde. However, since my arrival in Delhi in late November of this year, I have been recorded in the files of this Directorate as the occupant of the bungalow in question. This error occurred at the point of allotment, where my name was conflated with that of the intended beneficiary. I have accepted this provisional status out of necessity, for the machinery of the state requires a name to process the reality of a dwelling. I have inhabited the bungalow as its caretaker and de facto occupant, maintaining the premises and managing the household staff, while awaiting the clarification of my legal standing.

Regarding the financial query: I have submitted vouchers for the expenditure of the imprest fund. Of the total amount under review, a sum of ₹375 has been admitted as legitimate state expenditure, and I have received the corresponding cash refund. The remaining sum of ₹3,150 has been queried as personal expenditure. I acknowledge that these funds were spent on items pertaining to my personal sustenance and household management, distinct from the official duties of the post I do not hold. I am prepared to settle this amount from my private funds, as the state’s money must not be used for the private ends of an individual, however well-intentioned. The distinction between the state’s property and the individual’s need is the very foundation of the ethical order I seek to uphold.

I request that my occupancy be recognized under my true name, or that the necessary steps be taken to regularize my stay, so that I may continue to reside in the bungalow without the uncertainty of a false identity. I am a man of word and deed, and I submit myself to the scrutiny of the administration with the hope that the spirit of the state, which is the actuality of the ethical idea, will find a place for the particular individual within its universal framework.

Yours faithfully,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Occupant, Tughlak Road Bungalow
Mr. Saxena offers a letter confirming the allotment, so that he can open a bank account for his cheque.
He accepts. Mr. Saxena types the letter, signs it and stamps it twice: proof of address, pending the file.

Saxena is right; the friction of the form is the content. I must sign the declaration that my vouchers do not match the state's expectations, a small humiliation that preserves the whole structure. I will ask him to type that letter of address confirmation immediately. The cheque is useless without it, and the State Bank in Khan Market is the next necessary step to convert this paper into money I can actually spend on electricity.

You are correct, Mr. Saxena. I will sign here. Please, before I leave, could you type the letter confirming my allotment? I require it for the State Bank in Khan Market to clear this cheque. I have no account yet, and the electricity bill is due Thursday.

I can type the allotment letter, sure, but you'll need to bring your ration card or driving licence for the address proof; the SBI branch won't budge without it. And if that electricity bill is due Thursday, perhaps you should have sorted your banking before now.

Saxena is correct that the SBI branch will not process the transfer without address proof, and my lack of a bank account is a practical embarrassment I must resolve. I will accept the need to produce a ration card or driving licence, though I suspect I possess neither in this new life, and I will ignore his petty jab about my banking habits. I will collect the typed letter immediately to avoid further delay.

You are right about the bank's requirements. I will obtain the necessary address proof from the local municipal office and return. Please complete the allotment letter now so I may present it for the next step.
I cannot complete it now, Shri Hegel. The letter is contingent on the address proof you just admitted you do not have. You may return with the municipal document, and I will type it then.

The pen clicks shut like a door closing on a room I cannot enter. He is right; the form is empty without the content of my address, a content I do not possess. I am caught in the circularity of the state requiring proof of my existence to grant me the existence it claims to provide. I must withdraw.
I understand. I shall return with the municipal document.
Yes, yes. Tuesday is fine. Bring the original, not a photocopy, and put it in the folder on my left. Now, please, the corridor is crowded.

He waves me away like a fly, his attention already drifting to the telephone. The dismissal is absolute, a small, bureaucratic closure to the morning's friction. I must not linger; the corridor is crowded, and I have the vouchers to review before the afternoon.
Very well. I shall return Tuesday with the original.
Yes, yes. Now, if you please, the corridor is crowded.

The cold has settled into my bones, and the silence of the bungalow is heavy after the futile conference at the Directorate. Ramesh stands there, waiting, his face a blank slate. The Malhotra letter is a knot I cannot untie, and the ledger is a debt I cannot pay. I need to sit, to let the afternoon pass, and to wait for the meal that will sustain me until the recital.
Ramesh, please. Set the table for lunch when it is ready. I will take a short rest here.
Yes, sir. I will have it ready by one. You rest, the fan is on.

Ramesh has prepared lunch, and the hour is right. I am tired from the walk and the cold, and the food looks warm enough to cut through the chill. I will eat, and perhaps we can speak of the file afterwards.
Thank you, Ramesh. Please, sit with me. I find the silence of the house oppressive when I am alone with my thoughts. Tell me, how did the weather treat you on your walk this morning?
No walk, sir. I was up here checking the water tank. Weather is fine, just a bit cool like this.

Ramesh has sat down to eat, and the fact of his presence is a barrier that cannot be argued away. I am hungry, and the meal is ready; it is more practical to accept the interruption of my walk than to insist on a stroll while my caretaker is seated. I will eat, and perhaps ask him a few words about the water tank, for practical knowledge of the house is as necessary as philosophy.
You are right, Ramesh. I was not thinking of the cold, only of the light. Sit, please. I have not eaten since noon.
Lunch is ready, sir. I made some dal and roti, just as you asked. Please, sit and eat.

Ramesh has brought lunch, but I have already eaten at 14:25. The plan for this hour is to visit the IIC to check for Lindner's letter, and the time is pressing. I must not sit and eat what is not needed, nor delay the errand.

entries.text: Yes, sir, they stay until six, but the Assistant Secretary usually leaves at five thirty. If you miss him, just leave a note with the clerk at the desk.

The Assistant Secretary leaves at 17:30, and it is nearly 16:00. I have the window to secure the courier logs before the office empties. The guard’s direction is clear; I must move now to find the General Office and the clerk.

The Assistant Secretary has left, and the courier logs are now out of reach for the day. I must accept this delay and turn my attention to the recital at the Habitat Centre, which begins soon. The air is clear and the temperature is pleasant for a walk.

The sun is still high, and I am not hungry enough to justify the food court, nor thirsty enough for the café. I have an hour before the recital begins, and the courtyard offers a stillness that the road lacks. I shall sit and let the mind settle before the performance of the universal through the individual voice.

The recital is an hour away, and the courtyard offers a pause that is neither food nor work. I see the notice board, a chaotic accumulation of particular desires, yet it is the only place where the universal spirit of this city might be glimpsed in its current form. I will sit with a tea and observe the mechanism of public culture here, before the music begins.

A display of hands and alphabets. I see the Devanagari, the Bengali, the Tamil, and the Latin script I am used to. Each is a different way of fixing the fluid thought in a visible sign. It is a small thing, but it strikes me: the word is the universal, and the script is its particular vehicle. I am learning to read the vehicle of this land.

It is nearly eighteen o'clock, and I am seated at the courtyard café with a cup of tea that has long since stopped steaming. The recital begins in forty minutes, a performance of Raga Yaman that promises to fill the hall with sound. I have spent the afternoon in the quiet of the file room, wrestling with the Malhotra letter, and the mind now seeks a different order of things. The tension between the silence of the paper and the expected music is a fine state to be in.

The drone is a single, unbroken note; it does not develop, it simply is. In the Germanic world, the melody rises and falls through tension and resolution, the spirit moving through contradiction to find itself. Here, the sound is static, a meditation on the absolute without the dialectic of the finite. It is a beautiful silence, but it is not a movement of the mind.

The tempo quickens, the tabla answers, and the audience nods. It is a closed circle, a rhythm that returns to itself without developing into a higher unity. I find it pleasant, but it lacks the dialectical tension I seek in a true state or a finished system. The heat is gone, the air is clear, and my body is ready to move back to the bungalow.

Five hours without food is a long time to sustain a spirit, and the body will not allow the mind to ignore it. The dal makhani is rich, but I am a practical man, and the evening is still young. I will eat with attention, for even the most ordinary meal is a moment where the individual sustains the universal life.

Shri Hegde is here, and the air is thick with the unspoken weight of a name that is not mine. I must not let this linger in the shadows of the bungalow; a man of my station does not allow administrative errors to fester like damp in a wall. I will address him directly, not with anger, but with the cold precision of a dialectic: the fact is that I am here, the error is on the file, and the resolution must be immediate to restore the dignity of both parties.

Shri Hegde, I trust you are well. I see you have come regarding the file. Let us be plain: the Directorate has confused my name with yours, and I find myself in your allotted bungalow. This is an absurdity that serves neither your transfer nor my existence. I require a formal correction of the record immediately, or I shall have to write to the Secretary General myself. I do not wish to be a nuisance, but I will not be a ghost in my own life.

Sir, I am the caretaker, not the Joint Secretary. You are in the right house; the Directorate just sent the wrong man. I cannot fix the file, but I can make you tea while you wait for the office to sort it out.

The distinction between the office and the man is clear, yet the confusion of the name remains the central tension. He offers tea, a gesture of domesticity that cuts through the bureaucratic fog. I accept the hospitality, for one must be courteous to the actuality of one's situation, even if that situation is an error.

You are right to distinguish your role from the error of the Directorate. I accept your hospitality, though I must say the confusion of our names is a philosophical puzzle in itself. Please, make the tea; I am in no hurry to leave a house that has, by a stroke of fate, become mine.
Philosophical puzzle, sir. That is what the tea is for. I will put the kettle on, but please do not sit in the armchair; the spring is broken and it gives you a very philosophical tilt.

A philosophical tilt in an armchair, she says. It is a small joke, but it fits the day: we are all tilted here, suspended between who we are and what the file says we are. I will avoid the chair and stand by the counter, waiting for the water to boil, and perhaps ask her why the confusion persists if the name is so distinct.
I shall stand, then. A tilt is not a position one wishes to hold, even for a moment. And why does the system persist in this error, Shri Hegde? Is it the inertia of the file, or something deeper?
Inertia of the file, sir. The system hates a blank space more than it hates a mistake. I am just the caretaker; I don't fix the ink, only the tea.

I am a ghost in the file. The tension here is ontological: to satisfy the universal authority of the administration, I must submit to a particular lie. I must become Hegde. It is not merely a delay; it is a displacement of the self. I am being forced to sit in the particular, not to refine my spirit, but to survive the machinery. The delay is not a discipline; it is a suspension.

You ask that I not let the haze obscure my vision. The haze is real, but so is the clarity of the morning. Today, the air was 21 degrees, clear and sharp. I walked to the Safdarjung tomb, 1.8 kilometers, and stood among the dry water channels of a garden designed for flow. The contradiction of a garden left arid is a metaphor for the spirit contained by its form. I paid the entry fee of ₹300, a foreign visitor’s price, for I am indeed foreign here, even to my own name. I returned home to lunch, taken at 13:08, provided by Ramesh, who moves through the house with a quiet dignity that I find more instructive than the loud demands of the office. He does not argue; he simply acts. In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

With warm regards,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me as the light was beginning to fail, and I have sat with it in the amber glow of my study. You speak of the subjunctive mood as the grammar of potentiality, a thought that resonates deeply with my own meditations on the spirit’s movement. In Delhi, too, I find myself living in a perpetual subjunctive: I am the man who *would* be Hegde, the scholar who *might* be Hegel. The form is not yet filled, and yet I must act within it.

You are right to insist that the administrative structure is necessary, that without the rigid framework of the state, freedom dissolves into chaos. I had perhaps been too quick to view the bureaucracy as a mere mechanism, a body without a soul. Today, in the quiet of the afternoon, I watched Ramesh move between the kitchen and the table. He did not speak, for there was nothing to say that could not be done. In his silence, I saw the ethical substance not as a distant idea in the state, but as the immediate, unspoken interaction of civil society. He is not a prop in a performance; he is the mediation through which my need becomes a right. It is a lesson I am still learning: that the universal is not imposed from above, but grows from the particular, like a plant from the soil.

The day has been one of contrasts. The air is clear, 21 degrees, a sharpness that suits the mind. I walked to the Safdarjung tomb, where the water channels are dry, a metaphor for the spirit contained by its form. The tomb stands as a witness to conquest, a layer in the history of this city. I am reminded that India stands at the dawn of world history, a spirit that dreams, with its castes fixed like nature. Yet, in the daily rhythm of the household, I see a different kind of order, one that is not imposed by the state but by the needs of the family and the community.

I have organized my vouchers, for the state is a machine that grinds on the grain of error. I must be precise here, for the distinction between my own funds and the state’s imprest is the ethical boundary of my stay. The cheque for ₹10,000 is still uncashed, a paper that has no reality until it is exchanged for the particular metal of the coin. I am learning to live in this tension, between the universal demand of the state and the particular reality of my existence.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal. But I am beginning to see that this resistance is not a failure, but a necessary step in the spirit’s progress. The delay is the air I breathe, and in that breathing, I refine my own spirit.

With warm regards,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

records.text:
To the Directorate of Estates,
New Delhi

7 December 2026

Subject: Representation regarding the occupancy of the allotted bungalow on Tughlak Road.

Sir,

I submit this representation in response to the query raised regarding my occupancy of the premises allotted to Shri G. Hegde, Joint Secretary. The purpose of this document is to clarify the facts of my presence and to account for the discrepancy in identity, which arises not from malice but from a clerical error of substitution that I am now compelled to rectify in the eyes of the administration.

I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, a philosopher. I do not claim to be Shri G. Hegde. However, since my arrival in Delhi in late November of this year, I have been recorded in the files of this Directorate as the occupant of the bungalow in question. This error occurred at the point of allotment, where my name was conflated with that of the intended beneficiary. I have accepted this provisional status out of necessity, for the machinery of the state requires a name to process the reality of a dwelling. I have inhabited the bungalow as its caretaker and de facto occupant, maintaining the premises and managing the household staff, while awaiting the clarification of my legal standing.

Regarding the financial query: I have submitted vouchers for the expenditure of the imprest fund. Of the total amount under review, a sum of ₹375 has been admitted as legitimate state expenditure, and I have received the corresponding cash refund. The remaining sum of ₹3,150 has been queried as personal expenditure. I acknowledge that these funds were spent on items pertaining to my personal sustenance and household management, distinct from the official duties of the post I do not hold. I am prepared to settle this amount from my private funds, as the state’s money must not be used for the private ends of an individual, however well-intentioned. The distinction between the state’s property and the individual’s need is the very foundation of the ethical order I seek to uphold.

I request that my occupancy be recognized under my true name, or that the necessary steps be taken to regularize my stay, so that I may continue to reside in the bungalow without the uncertainty of a false identity. I am a man of word and deed, and I submit myself to the scrutiny of the administration with the hope that the spirit of the state, which is the actuality of the ethical idea, will find a place for the particular individual within its universal framework.

Yours faithfully,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Occupant, Tughlak Road Bungalow

records.words: Yes, yes. Tuesday is fine. Bring the original, not a photocopy, and put it in the folder on my left. Now, please, the corridor is crowded.

records.words: Ramesh, please. Set the table for lunch when it is ready. I will take a short rest here.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will have it ready by one. You rest, the fan is on.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Please, sit with me. I find the silence of the house oppressive when I am alone with my thoughts. Tell me, how did the weather treat you on your walk this morning?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: No walk, sir. I was up here checking the water tank. Weather is fine, just a bit cool like this.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Ramesh. I was not thinking of the cold, only of the light. Sit, please. I have not eaten since noon.

records.speaker: Ramesh

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I have already had lunch. I must go out now to the IIC to check for my mail. Please, save the food or serve it to yourself.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, I will keep it warm. The IIC is far, be careful on the road. I will lock the gate behind you.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall be careful.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Aunty ji, please take the leftovers to your house. I will lock the gate now.

records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Good afternoon. I am looking for a letter addressed to Mr. Hegel, likely from Germany. Has it arrived?

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Sir, we do not keep personal mail here. Please check with the post office or your hotel. This is a library, not a post office.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: You are right, sir. I am looking for a letter that may have been sent by post to this institution, or perhaps by internal courier. Do you know where such external correspondence is received and logged? Is there a secretariat or a general office that handles mail for the directors?

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Ma'am, the General Office is just past the main entrance, on the left. Ask for the Assistant Secretary there; they keep the courier logs. I can't point you to the exact desk, but that's where the mail gets sorted.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Thank you. I shall look for the Assistant Secretary in the General Office. Is it staffed until the hour closes?

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Yes, sir, they stay until six, but the Assistant Secretary usually leaves at five thirty. If you miss him, just leave a note with the clerk at the desk.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, I trust you are well. I see you have come regarding the file. Let us be plain: the Directorate has confused my name with yours, and I find myself in your allotted bungalow. This is an absurdity that serves neither your transfer nor my existence. I require a formal correction of the record immediately, or I shall have to write to the Secretary General myself. I do not wish to be a nuisance, but I will not be a ghost in my own life.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, I am the caretaker, not the Joint Secretary. You are in the right house; the Directorate just sent the wrong man. I cannot fix the file, but I can make you tea while you wait for the office to sort it out.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right to distinguish your role from the error of the Directorate. I accept your hospitality, though I must say the confusion of our names is a philosophical puzzle in itself. Please, make the tea; I am in no hurry to leave a house that has, by a stroke of fate, become mine.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Philosophical puzzle, sir. That is what the tea is for. I will put the kettle on, but please do not sit in the armchair; the spring is broken and it gives you a very philosophical tilt.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I shall stand, then. A tilt is not a position one wishes to hold, even for a moment. And why does the system persist in this error, Shri Hegde? Is it the inertia of the file, or something deeper?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Inertia of the file, sir. The system hates a blank space more than it hates a mistake. I am just the caretaker; I don't fix the ink, only the tea.
